section_summary: This section documents diplomatic reports and State Department analyses from December 1931 to February 1932 detailing the collapse of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and the formation of the Inukai administration in Japan. It features comprehensive studies of the Japanese military's autonomous constitutional status, focusing on the right of direct access to the Emperor (iaku joso) and its decisive role in precipitating and expanding the Manchurian incident without civilian control. Later papers examine the appointment of Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Chief of the Army General Staff to curb junior officer insubordination, the political fallout from a Korean assassination attempt on Emperor Hirohito, and civil-military conflict over continental policy.

subfiles.about: Analyzes the political crisis surrounding the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and evaluates the prospects of a successor ministry under Baron Wakatsuki or Seiyukai leader Tsuyoshi Inukai.
subfiles.summary: Reviews reports from the Tokyo Embassy indicating that the resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet was caused by internal political intrigue instigated by Home Minister Adachi rather than government policies. Considers whether Baron Wakatsuki or Seiyukai president Tsuyoshi Inukai will receive the Imperial mandate to form the new cabinet. Emphasizes the Seiyukai's hardline continental stance, quoting a November 1931 party resolution declaring Manchuria and Mongolia the life-blood of the Japanese Empire and threatening withdrawal from the League of Nations if international intervention persists.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese Cabinet Crisis and the Manchurian Situation

subfiles.about: Records the charging out of file items by State Department personnel between October 1968 and June 1969.
subfiles.summary: Department of State Form DS-1033 recording items charged out from file 894.00. Notes that records were charged out to Grandson on October 17, 1968, May 7, 1969, and June 2, 1969.
subfiles.title: Charge Out Record (Form DS-1033)

subfiles.about: Reports the collapse of the Wakatsuki Cabinet due to Home Minister Adachi's maneuvers, the formation of the Inukai Cabinet, its immediate policy moves including the reimposition of the gold embargo, and transmits biographic data on new ministers.
subfiles.summary: Details the political intrigue leading to the fall of the Minseito Cabinet of Baron Wakatsuki, highlighting Home Minister Adachi's unauthorized demand for a coalition government and possible financial backing from Mitsui interests anticipating a gold embargo. Describes Prince Saionji's recommendation of Seiyukai president Tsuyoshi Inukai, the formation of the new cabinet, and the immediate reimposition of the gold export embargo. Analyzes military and financial influences, the prospect of Diet dissolution, and encloses confidential biographic sketches of Ministers Sadao Araki, Tsuyoshi Inukai, Mineo Osumi, Ichiro Hatoyama, Tokugoro Nakabashi, and Takejiro Tokonami.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 422: Resignation of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and Formation of the Inukai Cabinet

subfiles.about: Presents a comprehensive study of the autonomous power of the Japanese military, focusing on the constitutional right of direct access to the Emperor (iaku joso) and its direct role in the Manchurian incident.
subfiles.summary: Examines the system of direct Imperial access (iaku joso) exercised by the Chiefs of Staff of the Army and Navy and other senior commanders, enabling them to obtain Imperial sanction for military actions and war plans without Cabinet knowledge or approval. Demonstrates how this institutional independence allowed the Kwantung Army to initiate and expand military operations at Mukden on September 18, 1931, completely bypassing civilian officials such as Foreign Minister Shidehara. Traces the origins of military autonomy to the Meiji Restoration, samurai traditions, and Prussian military models, reviewing constitutional analyses by Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe and Dr. Shinkichi Uesugi and confidential disclosures by Viscount Kentaro Kaneko, a co-drafter of the Meiji Constitution.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 423: The Autonomous Power of the Japanese Army and the Right of Direct Access to the Emperor

subfiles.about: Conveys the State Department's commendation of Second Secretary Laurence E. Salisbury for his preparation of Despatch No. 423 on the autonomous power of the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges receipt of Ambassador Forbes's strictly confidential Despatch No. 423 of December 18, 1931, concerning the autonomous power of the Japanese Army. Praises the despatch as excellent in form and substance, demonstrating intimate knowledge of an intricate subject and excellent contacts. Requests that the author, Second Secretary Salisbury, be officially commended.
subfiles.title: Instruction Commending Second Secretary Laurence E. Salisbury for Despatch No. 423

subfiles.about: Cross-references Tokyo Telegram No. 2 of January 8, 1932, regarding Japanese Cabinet deliberations on whether to resign.
subfiles.summary: State Department Document File Note indexing Tokyo Telegram No. 2 of January 8, 1932 (filed under 894.001H61/58) into decimal file 894.00/339. Notes that the Japanese Cabinet was in emergency session to discuss resigning following an attack on the Emperor, expecting a decision late that evening.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Cross-Reference to Telegram No. 2 Regarding Possible Cabinet Resignation

subfiles.about: Reports an attempted assassination of Emperor Hirohito by a Korean bomb thrower and notes that the Cabinet convened to deliberate resigning.
subfiles.summary: Reports that as Emperor Hirohito returned from the Imperial military review, a young Korean threw a bomb that exploded behind a carriage carrying an Imperial Household official, causing no injuries. Informs the Department that Ambassador Forbes conveyed condolences and congratulations on the Emperor's escape through Vice Minister Nagai and signed the Imperial Palace register. States that the Cabinet convened in emergency session to decide whether to tender its resignation over the security failure, awaiting the return of the absent Home Minister.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Telegram No. 2: Bombing Incident Targeting the Imperial Procession and Cabinet Resignation Deliberations

subfiles.about: Cross-references Secretary of State Stimson's memorandum of conversation with Count Kabayama regarding Japanese constitutional flaws and civil-military conflict.
subfiles.summary: State Department Document File Note indexing a memorandum dated January 8, 1932, filed under decimal file 793.94/3477. Summarizes a conversation in which Count Kabayama explained to Secretary Stimson the structural defects of the Japanese constitution, problems arising from the doctrine of Imperial sanctity, and the bitter conflict between the Japanese Army and civilian government.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: Cross-Reference to Secretary Stimson's Memorandum of Conversation with Count Kabayama

subfiles.about: Summarizes and assesses Tokyo Despatch No. 440 concerning the appointment of Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Chief of Staff and character sketches of prominent army officers.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Despatch No. 440 prepared by Second Secretary Salisbury regarding the appointment of Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Chief of the Army General Staff. Analyzes how selecting an Imperial Prince aimed to discipline insubordinate younger officers while neutralizing civilian moderates like Count Makino. Outlines the profile of new War Minister Sadao Araki as a popular chauvinist convinced that Japan must aggressively secure its continental position or risk being driven out of Manchuria by China.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 440 Regarding Prince Kanin and Prominent Army Leaders

subfiles.about: Reports the replacement of General Kanaya by Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Army Chief of Staff and transmits Japanese articles analyzing military leadership, factionalism, and civil-military discord.
subfiles.summary: Reports the resignation of General Kanaya and the appointment of Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Chief of the Army General Staff, discussing how Kanin's imperial status was intended to curb insubordination among young officers and further sideline civilian advisers like Count Makino. Relates an account that Kanaya resigned because past assurances to the Throne on defensive troop withdrawals from Chinchow prevented him from seeking sanction for renewed offensives. Encloses biographic data on Prince Kanin, a Kaizo article by Tatsuo Iwabuchi analyzing Sadao Araki's spiritual influence and Kuniaki Koiso's administrative control over the army, and a Chuo Koron article by Joji Takayama describing the General Staff's dominance over the Foreign Office and the collapse of Shidehara's conciliatory diplomacy.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 440: Appointment of Field Marshal Prince Kanin as Chief of Staff and Military Ascendancy
